s001.heard: NCERT opens its chapter on rights with two true stories. One is about a man named Machal Lalung. He was held in judicial custody for fifty-four years. He was released in 2005.

s002.heard: Article twenty-one says no one can lose life or liberty, except by procedure established by law. So can any law take your liberty, as long as it follows its own procedure?

s003.heard: This is part two of three on Fundamental Rights. Part one was equality. This part is freedom. First the six freedoms and their limits. Then life and liberty, and how one phrase in Article twenty-one changed its meaning.

s004.heard: Article nineteen gives citizens six freedoms. To speak and express yourself. To gather peacefully, without arms. To form associations or unions. To move freely across India. To live and settle anywhere in it. And to practise any profession, trade or business.

s005.heard: But no freedom here is absolute. Each comes with its own limits. Speech can be restricted for the sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, public order, decency or morality. Defamation, contempt of court and incitement to an offence are grounds too. And movement can be limited in the public interest, or to protect a Scheduled Tribe's interests.

s006.heard: A restriction must still be reasonable, and courts check that. In twenty fifteen, the Supreme Court struck down Section sixty-six A of the Information Technology Act in full. It held the section violated free speech and was not saved by the allowed limits.

s007.heard: Article twenty protects anyone accused of a crime. You cannot be punished for an act that was not an offence when you did it. You cannot be prosecuted and punished twice for the same offence. And you cannot be forced to be a witness against yourself.

s008.heard: Now, Article twenty-one. Life and liberty can go only by procedure established by law. In nineteen fifty, in the Gopalan case, a majority of the Court read each right as a separate box. On that reading, a law that set out a procedure could be enough. NCERT's Class Nine glossary says the phrase means strict adherence to duly enacted and valid laws. To our ear, that is the Gopalan idea.

s009.heard: But in nineteen seventy-eight, Maneka Gandhi's passport was impounded, at first without reasons. Seven judges heard her case. Six joined the lead opinion. The procedure must be right, just and fair, not arbitrary. One judge dissented. It must also pass the test of equality in Article fourteen. And the rights are not separate boxes. Later judges said they overlap.

s010.heard: So Article twenty-one grew wider and wider. Take privacy. The word privacy does not appear anywhere in the Constitution. Yet on the twenty-fourth of August, twenty seventeen, nine judges decided it together. Privacy is protected under Article twenty-one, and by the other freedoms.

s011.heard: But privacy is not absolute either. The lead opinion, for four judges, set a three-part test. A law must exist. It must serve a legitimate aim. And the means must be proportionate to that aim. The same opinion said privacy covers your data, with dangers from the State and from others. A data protection law came in twenty-twenty-three, and comes into force in stages.

s012.heard: Article twenty-one kept widening. Education became its own right in Article twenty-one A, for children aged six to fourteen. NCERT's Class Nine book says it was added in two thousand nine. The amendment is of two thousand two, in force from two thousand ten. The Court also held that the right to life includes livelihood. And it read clean water and air into it.

s013.heard: What if you are arrested? Article twenty-two says you must be told why, as soon as possible. You may consult a lawyer of your choice. And you must be taken before the nearest magistrate within twenty-four hours. In nineteen ninety-six, the Court added rules for every arrest, a memo of arrest, and a relative or friend told.

s014.heard: But there is a harder case, preventive detention, to stop a feared act before it happens. The Constitution allows it, with a check. Detention beyond three months needs an Advisory Board's report, unless a law of Parliament provides otherwise. A nineteen seventy-eight amendment would cut that to two months. But in the Legislative Department's text of September twenty-twenty-six, that change is still not in force.

s015.heard: And during an Emergency? The President may suspend the right to go to court for most Fundamental Rights. But not for Articles twenty and twenty-one. That exception was added in nineteen seventy-eight. In twenty seventeen came Puttaswamy. Its lead opinion, for four judges, overruled the Emergency-era ruling of nineteen seventy-six, ADM Jabalpur.

s016.heard: Freedom also means freedom from exploitation. Article twenty-three bans trafficking in people, and forced labour. In nineteen eighty-two, workers building for the Asian Games were paid below the minimum wage. The Supreme Court held that this was forced labour. And it held that the Article binds private contractors too.

s017.heard: Article twenty-four bars children under fourteen from factories, mines and other hazardous work. And NCERT Class Eight says a law in force from December twenty thirteen bans employing people as manual scavengers.

s018.heard: So can any law take your liberty, as long as it follows its own procedure? Since Maneka Gandhi, no. The procedure itself must be fair, just and reasonable, and must pass the test of equality. And since Puttaswamy, a law that touches privacy needs a legitimate aim and proportionate means. That is the lead opinion, for four judges.

s019.heard: For the exam, write it this way. Article nineteen gives six freedoms, each with reasonable restrictions. Article twenty protects the accused. Article twenty-one, after Maneka Gandhi, needs fair procedure. It now holds privacy, livelihood, and clean water and air. And Article twenty-one A adds education.

s020.heard: In part three, religion, culture and education. Then the right to move the Court, and the Directive Principles that guide the State.
